technical-data.invention-title: IMPROVED INSTRUCTION DECODING USING A PARALLEL DECODE ALGORITHM
DECODAGE D'INSTRUCTIONS AMELIORE UTILISANT UN ALGORITHME DE DECODAGE PARALLELE

abstract.p: A predecode unit (17) is configured to predecode a fixed number of instruction bytes of variable length instructions per clock cycle. The predecode unit outputs predecode bits which identify whether any of the predecoded instruction bytes are the start byte of an instruction. An instruction alignment unit (18) then uses the start bits to dispatch the variable byte-length instructions to a plurality of decode units (20) that form fixed issue positions within a processor. In one embodiment, the predecode unit identifies a plurality of length vectors. Each length vector is associated with one of the instruction bytes predecoded in a clock cycle. The length vector identifies the length of an instruction if an instruction starts at the instruction byte corresponding to the length vector. A tree circuit (312) determines in which instruction bytes instructions start.

L'invention concerne une unité de prédécodage (17) configurée pour prédécoder un nombre déterminé d'octets d'instructions de longueur variable par cycle d'horloge. L'unité de prédécodage sort des bits de prédécodage déterminant si un des octets d'instructions prédécodées est un octet de lancement d'une instruction. Une unité d'alignement d'instruction (18) utilise ensuite les bits de départ pour envoyer les instructions à longueur-octet variable à une pluralité d'unités de décodage (20) qui forment des positions de sortie fixe dans un processeur. Selon une variante, l'unité de prédécodage identifie une pluralité de vecteurs de longueur. Chaque vecteur est associé à un des octets d'instructions prédécodées dans un cycle d'horloge. Le vecteur de longueur identifie la longueur d'une instruction si une instruction débute au niveau de l'octet d'instruction correspondant au vecteur de longueur. Un circuit en arborescence (312) détermine dans quels octets d'instructions débutent les instructions.

description.p: Title: IMPROVED INSTRUCTION DECODING USING A PARALLEL DECODE ALGORITHM
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

1. Technical Field This invention relates to superscalar microprocessors and, more particularly, to the predecoding of vaπable byte-length computer instructions within high performance and high frequency superscalar microprocessors.

2 Background Art Superscalar microprocessors are capable of attaining performance characteristics which surpass those of conventional scalar processors by allowing the concurrent execution of multiple instructions. Due to the widespread acceptance of the x86 family of microprocessors, efforts have been undertaken by microprocessor manufacturers to develop superscalar microprocessors that execute x86 instructions. Such superscalar microprocessors achieve relatively high performance characteristics while advantageously maintaining backwards compatibility with the vast amount of existing software developed for previous microprocessor generations such as the 8086, 80286, 80386, 80486, Pentium™ , K5™, Pentium II™, and K6™

The x86 instruction set is relatively complex and is characterized by a plurality of variable byte-length instructions A generic format illustrative of the x86 instruction set is shown m Figure 1A. As illustrated in the figure, an x86 instruction consists of from one to fourteen optional prefix bytes 102, followed by an operation code (opcode) field 104, an optional addressing mode (ModR/M) byte 106, an optional scale-mdex-base (SIB) byte 108, an optional displacement field 110, and an optional immediate data field 112.

The opcode field 104 defines the basic operation for a particular instruction. The default operation of a particular opcode may be modified by one or more prefix bytes For example, a prefix byte may be used to change the address or operand size for an instruction, to override the default segment used m memory addressing, or to instruct the processor to repeat a string operation a number of times The opcode field 104 follows the prefix bytes 102, if any, and may be one or two bytes in length. The addressing mode (ModR/M) byte 106 specifies the registers used as well as memory addressing modes. The register field of the ModR/M byte alternatively may be used as an opcode extension, or sub-opcode. The scale-mdex-base (SIB) byte 108 is used only in 32-bit base-relative addressing usmg scale and index factors. A base field ofthe SIB byte specifies which register contains the base value for the address calculation, and an mdex field specifies which register contains the mdex value. A scale field specifies the power of two by which the mdex value will be multiplied before being added, along with any displacement, to the base value. The next instruction field is the optional displacement field 110. which may be from one to four bytes m length. The displacement field 110 contains a constant used in address calculations. The optional immediate field 1 12, which may also be from one to six bytes in length, contains a constant used as an instruction operand. The 80286 sets a maximum length for an instruction at 10 bytes, while the 80386, 80486, Pentium™, K5™, Pentium II™. and K6™ allow instruction lengths of up to 15 bytes

Referring now to Figure IB, several different vaπable byte-length x86 instruction formats are shown The shortest x86 instruction is only one byte long, and comprises a single opcode byte as shown in format (a)
For certam mstructions, the byte contammg the opcode field also contams a register field as shown m formats (b), (c) and (e). Format 0) shows an instruction with two opcode bytes. An optional ModR/M byte follows opcode bytes m formats (d), (f), (h), and 0)- Immediate data follows opcode bytes m formats (e), (g), (l), and (k), and follows a ModR/M byte in formats (f) and (h). Figure IC illustrates several possible addressing mode formats (a)-(h) Formats (c), (d), (e), (g), and (h) contam ModR/M bytes with offset (i.e., displacement) information. An SIB byte is used in formats (f), (g), and (h).

The complexity ofthe x86 mstruction set poses difficulties in implementing high performance x86 compatible superscalar microprocessors. One difficulty aπses from the fact that mstructions must be aligned with respect to the parallel-coupled instruction decoders of such processors before proper decode can be effectuated In contrast to most RISC mstruction formats, since the x86 mstruction set consists of vaπable byte- length mstructions, the start bytes of successive mstructions within a lme are not necessaπly equally spaced, and the number of mstructions per lme is not fixed. As a result, employment of simple, fixed- length shifting logic cannot in itself solve the problem of mstruction alignment.

Superscalar microprocessors have been proposed that employ mstruction predecodmg techniques to help solve the problem of quickly aligning, decodmg and executing a plurality of vaπable byte-length instructions in parallel. In one such superscalar microprocessor, when mstructions are written withm the mstruction cache from an external mam memory, a predecoder appends several predecode bits (referred to collectively as a predecode tag) to each byte. These bits may mdicate whether the byte is the start and/or end byte of an x86 instruction, the number of microinstructions required to implement the x86 mstruction, and the location of opcodes and prefixes. Unfortunately, predecode units expeπence the same difficulties in aligning mstructions as decode units.

In one implementation, a predecode unit attempts to predecode one instruction per clock cycle. A multiplexer routes instruction bytes to the predecode unit, which determines the length of the mstruction and routes the mstruction length to the multiplexer, which routes the bytes subsequent to the previously predecoded mstruction to the predecode unit to be predecoded m the next clock cycle. Because the mstruction length is vaπable, the multiplexer must be able to shift the mstruction bytes from 1 to 15 bytes, which mcreases the complexity of the multiplexer Further, the time to detect the length ofthe instruction, route the mstruction length to the multiplexer, and shift the mstruction bytes by the appropπate number of positions is a tune consuming operation that may limit the performance of the predecode unit and consequently limit the performance ofthe microprocessor.
DISCLOSURE OF INVENTION

The problems outlmed above are in large part solved by a predecode unit configured to predecode a fixed number of mstruction bytes of vaπable length mstructions per clock cycle. The predecode unit outputs predecode bits which identify whether any ofthe predecoded mstruction bytes are the start byte of an mstruction. An mstruction alignment unit then uses the start bits to dispatch the vaπable byte-length instructions to a plurality of decode units that form fixed issue positions withm a processor By predecodmg a fixed number of instruction bytes per clock cycle, the multiplexer that routes instruction bytes to the predecode umt shifts mstructions bytes by a fixed number, which greatly simplifies the multiplexer. Furthermore, the multiplexing operation may be performed m parallel with the predecode operation because the number of byte
positions by which the multiplexer shifts the mstruction bytes is mdependent ofthe predecode operation. Both of these features accommodate very high frequencies of operation.

In one embodiment, the predecode unit identifies a plurality of length vectors. Each length vector is associated with one of the mstruction bytes predecoded m a clock cycle. The length vector identifies the length of an mstruction if an mstruction starts at the mstruction byte correspondmg to the length vector. A tree circuit determines in which mstruction bytes mstructions start The length vector correspondmg to the mstruction byte in which an mstruction starts identifies the mstruction byte m which a subsequent mstruction starts (i.e., the subsequent start byte) If the subsequent start byte is outside of the fixed number of mstruction bytes predecoded durmg that clock cycle, the tree circuit stores the information until the subsequent start byte is predecoded. The length vector associated with the subsequent start byte is then used to determine the instruction byte in which the next mstruction starts.

By utilizing the predecoded information from the predecode unit, the instruction alignment unit may be implemented with a relatively small number of cascaded levels of logic gates, thus accommodating very high frequencies of operation Instruction alignment to decode units may further be accomplished with relatively few pipeline stages. Broadly speaking, the present invention contemplates a predecode unit mcludmg a decode circuit, a prefix find circuit, a prefix accumulator and a tree circuit. The decode circuit is configured to decode a fixed number of instruction bytes m a clock cycle and to output a plurality of mstruction length vectors The prefix find circuit is configured to receive said fixed number of mstruction bytes and to identify which of said fixed number of mstruction bytes are prefixes The prefix accumulator circuit is coupled to said decode circuit and said prefix find circuit, and is configured to output a plurality of position length vectors which identify an instruction length for potential start bytes. The tree circuit is coupled to said prefix accumulation circuit, and is configured to output a plurality of start bits The start bits identify one or more start bytes withm said fixed number of instruction bytes.

The present invention further contemplates a method of predecodmg mstruction bytes of vaπable-byte length instructions to identify start bytes of vaπable length instructions compnsmg. predecodmg a fixed number of mstruction bytes starting with an instruction byte identified by a predecode pomter, wherein said predecodmg identifies said start bytes withm said fixed number of mstruction bytes; mcrementmg said predecode pomter by said fixed number of mstruction bytes; and predecodmg said fixed number of mstruction bytes starting with an mstruction byte identified by said predecode pointer. The present invention still further contemplates a method of predecodmg mstruction bytes of variable- byte length mstructions to identify start bytes of variable length mstructions compnsmg: determining a first instruction length if a start byte is m a first byte position; determining a second mstruction length if said start byte is m a second byte position, determining a location of a first start byte based upon an mstruction byte position of a previous start byte and an mstruction length associated with said previous start position; and selecting said first instruction length if said first start byte is m said first byte position and selectmg said second mstruction byte length if said first start byte is in said second byte position.

In one embodiment, the predecode unit predecodes four mstmction bytes per clock cycle. The predecode unit determines a length vector for each ofthe four mstruction bytes. The length vector identifies the length of an mstruction if an mstruction starts m the mstmction byte correspondmg to the length vector. It is noted that the predecode unit may additionally provide predecode bits which identify the end of an mst ction, the type of mstmction, and other information.

Instruction cache 16 is a high speed cache memory provided to store mstructions. Instructions are fetched from mstmction cache 16 and dispatched to decode umts 20. In one embodiment, mstmction cache 16 is configured to store up to 64 kilobytes of instructions m a two-way set associative structure having 64 byte lmes (a byte comprises 8 binary bits). In this manner, the way is selected pnor to accessmg the mstruction storage. The access time of mstmction cache 16 may be similar to a direct-mapped cache. A tag companson is performed and, if the way prediction is lncoπect, the coπect mstructions are fetched and the incorrect mstructions are discarded. If the mstructions received from instruction cache 16 have not been predecoded, the instructions

In the exemplary encodmg, if a given byte is the first byte of an mstruction, the start bit for that byte is set If the byte is the last byte of an mstmction, the end bit for that byte is set Instructions which may be directly decoded by decode units 20 are referred to as "fast path" instructions The remaining x86 mstmctions are refeπed to as MROM mstructions, accordmg to one embodiment For fast path mstmctions, the functional bit is asserted for the first instruction byte Alternatively, for MROM mstructions, the functional bit is unasserted for the first instruction byte The type of mstmction may be determined by exammmg the functional bit coπesponding to the first mstmction byte Prefix bytes are identified by an asserted functional bit m the position coπesponding to the subsequent mstmction byte For example, if the first mstmction byte is a prefix byte the second functional bit is asserted The opcode of an mstmction may thereby be located withm an instruction as the byte associated with the last asserted functional bit m the mstmction For example, a fast path instruction including two prefix bytes, an opcode, a ModR/M byte, and an immediate byte would have start, end, and functional bits as follows

Accordmg to one particular embodiment, early identification of an mstmction that mcludes a scale- mdex-base (SIB) byte is advantageous for MROM unit 34 For such an embodiment, if an mstmction includes at least two bytes after the opcode byte, the functional bit for the ModR/M byte indicates the presence of an SIB byte If the functional bit for the ModR/M byte is set, then an SIB byte is present Alternatively, if the functional bit for the ModR/M byte is clear, then an SIB byte is not present

MROM mstmctions are mstmctions which are determined to be too complex for decode by decode units 20 MROM mstmctions are executed by invoking MROM unit 34 More specifically, when an MROM instruction is encountered, MROM unit 34 parses
and issues the mstmction mto a subset of defined fast path instructions to effectuate the desired operation. MROM unit 34 dispatches the subset of fast path mstmctions to decode units 20

Microprocessor 10 employs branch prediction m order to speculatively fetch mstmctions subsequent to conditional branch mstmctions. Branch prediction unit 14 is mcluded to perform branch prediction operations. In one embodiment, up to two branch target addresses are stored with respect to each 16 byte portion of each cache lme in mstmction cache 16 Predecode unit 17 determines initial branch targets when a particular lme is predecoded. Subsequent updates to the branch targets coπesponding to a cache lme may occur due to the execution of mstructions withm the cache lme. Instruction cache 16 provides an indication ofthe mstruction address being fetched, so that branch prediction unit 14 may determine which branch target addresses to select for forming a branch prediction. Decode units 20 and functional units 24 provide update information to branch prediction unit 14 Because branch prediction unit 14 stores two targets per 16 byte portion ofthe cache lme, some branch mstmctions withm the lme may not be stored m branch prediction unit 14. Decode units 20 detect branch mstmctions which were not predicted by branch prediction unit 14. Functional units 24 execute the branch mstmctions and determine if the predicted branch direction is mcoπect. The branch direction may be "taken", m which subsequent mstructions are fetched from the target address ofthe branch mstmction Conversely, the branch direction may be "not taken", m which subsequent mstmctions are fetched from memory locations consecutive to the branch mstmction. When a mispredicted branch mstruction is detected, mstmctions subsequent to the mispredicted branch are discarded from the vaπous units of microprocessor 10 A vanety of suitable branch prediction algorithms may be employed by branch prediction unit 14

Instructions fetched from instruction cache 16 are conveyed to mst ction alignment unit 18. As mstmctions are fetched from mstmction cache 16, the coπesponding predecode data is scanned to provide information to mstruction alignment unit 18 (and to MROM unit 34) regardmg the mstmctions bemg fetched. Instruction alignment unit 18 utilizes the scanning data to align an mstmction to each of decode units 20. In one embodiment, instruction alignment unit 18 aligns mstmctions from three sets of eight mstmction bytes to decode units 20. Instructions are selected mdependently from each set of eight mstmction bytes mto preliminary issue positions The preliminary issue positions are then merged to a set of aligned issue positions coπesponding to decode units 20, such that the aligned issue positions contam the three mstmctions which are pnor to other instructions withm the prelunmary issue positions m program order Decode umt 20A receives an mstruction which is pnor to mstmctions concuπently received by decode units 20B and 20C (in program order) Similarly, decode unit 20B receives an mstmction which is pnor to the mstmction concuπently received by decode unit 20C m program order.

Decode units 20 are configured to decode mstmctions received from mstruction alignment unit 18 Register operand information is detected and routed to register file 30 and reorder buffer 32. Additionally, if the mstmctions require one or more memory operations to be performed, decode units 20 dispatch the memory operations to load/store unit 26. Each mstmction is decoded mto a set of control values for functional units 24, and these control values are dispatched to reservation stations 22 along with operand address information and displacement or immediate data which may be mcluded with the mstmction.

Microprocessor 10 supports out of order execution, and thus employs reorder buffer 32 to keep track of the oπgmal program sequence for register read and wnte operations, to implement register renaming, to allow for speculative mstmction execution and branch misprediction recovery, and to facilitate precise exceptions A
temporary storage location withm reorder buffer 32 is reserved upon decode of an mstruction that mvolves the update of a register to thereby store speculative register states. If a branch prediction is mcoπect, the results of speculatively-executed mstmctions along the mispredicted path can be invalidated m the buffer before they are wπtten to register file 30. Similarly, if a particular mstmction causes an exception, mstmctions subsequent to the particular mstmction may be discarded. In this manner, exceptions are "precise" (i.e. mstmctions subsequent to the particular mstmction causmg the exception are not completed pnor to the exception). It is noted that a particular mstmction is speculatively executed if it is executed pnor to mstmctions which precede the particular mstmction m program order Precedmg mstructions may be a branch mstmction or an exception- causing mstmction, in which case the speculative results may be discarded by reorder buffer 32

The mstmction control values and immediate or displacement data provided at the outputs of decode units 20 are routed directly to respective reservation stations 22. In one embodiment, each reservation station 22 is capable of holdmg mstmction information (I e., instruction control values as well as operand values, operand tags and/or immediate data) for up to three pending mstmctions awaiting issue to the coπespondmg functional unit It is noted that for the embodiment of Figure 1, each reservation station 22 is associated with a dedicated functional unit 24 Accordmgly, three dedicated "issue positions" are formed by reservation stations 22 and functional umts 24. In other words, issue position 0 is formed by reservation station 22 A and functional unit 24A Instructions aligned and dispatched to reservation station 22A are executed by functional unit 24A. Similarly, issue position 1 is formed by reservation station 22B and functional unit 24B; and issue position 2 is formed by reservation station 22C and functional unit 24C.

Upon decode of a particular mstmction, if a required operand is a register location, register address information is routed to reorder buffer 32 and register file 30 simultaneously. Those of skill m the art will appreciate that the x86 register file mcludes eight 32 bit real registers (i.e., typically refeπed to as EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX, EBP, ESI, EDI and ESP) In embodiments of microprocessor 10 which employ the x86 microprocessor architecture, register file 30 comprises storage locations for each ofthe 32 bit real registers. Additional storage locations may be mcluded withm register file 30 for use by MROM unit 34 Reorder buffer 32 contams temporary storage locations for results which change the contents of these registers to thereby allow out of order execution. A temporary storage location of reorder buffer 32 is reserved for each mstmction which, upon decode, is determined to modify the contents of one of the real registers. Therefore, at vaπous pomts during execution of a particular program, reorder buffer 32 may have one or more locations which contam the speculatively executed contents of a given register If following decode of a given instruction it is determined that reorder buffer 32 has a previous location or locations assigned to a register used as an operand in the given mstmction, the reorder buffer 32 forwards to the coπespondmg reservation station either 1) the value m the most recently assigned location, or 2) a tag for the most recently assigned location if the value has not yet been produced by the functional unit that will eventually execute the previous mstmction. If reorder buffer 32 has a location reserved for a given register, the operand value (or reorder buffer tag) is provided from reorder buffer 32 rather than from register file 30 If there is no location reserved for a required register in reorder buffer 32, the value is taken directly from register file 30 If the operand coπesponds to a memory location, the operand value is provided to the reservation station through load/store unit 26.
